title: NRI Deposit Surge Drives India's July Balance of Payments to $20.8B Surplus
excerpt: Capital account inflows hit $27.7 billion as the RBI's deposit schemes pulled in $136.4 billion, while the current account deficit widened to $7 billion on a larger trade gap.
body:
• India's balance of payments flipped to a $20.8 billion surplus in July, from $0.3 billion a year earlier, on a surge of foreign-exchange inflows.
  • The capital account logged a $27.7 billion net inflow versus $3.5 billion a year ago, with net NRI deposits surging to $33.5 billion from $1 billion.
  • Net transfers, including remittances from Indian workers overseas, rose to $13.2 billion; foreign direct investment climbed to $7.3 billion and portfolio flows turned positive at $4.1 billion.
  • The RBI's June 5 incentive schemes mobilised $136.4 billion through August 31, including $127 billion from non-resident deposits.

India's balance of payments recorded a $20.8 billion surplus in July, compared with a surplus of just $0.3 billion a year earlier, as a surge in foreign-exchange inflows overwhelmed a widening trade gap. Preliminary data released by the Reserve Bank of India on September 15 showed the capital account logging a net inflow of $27.7 billion — nearly eight times the $3.5 billion recorded in July 2025.

The standout number was diaspora money. Net NRI deposits surged to $33.5 billion in July from $1 billion a year earlier, according to ANI, as overseas Indians poured dollars into the RBI's concessional deposit schemes. Banking capital recorded a net inflow of $18.4 billion, up from $6 billion, while net foreign direct investment rose to $7.3 billion from $4.5 billion and net foreign portfolio investment turned positive at $4.1 billion — against an outflow of $2.5 billion a year earlier.

The trade side still bleeds

The financing side more than offset weakness on the current account, where the deficit widened to $7 billion from $3.2 billion a year ago. The merchandise trade deficit stretched to $31.7 billion from $28.2 billion: exports rose to $45.1 billion from $37.4 billion, but imports increased faster, to $76.8 billion from $65.6 billion. For April–July, the merchandise trade deficit stood at $117.8 billion versus $97.1 billion a year earlier.

Services provided some offset. Net services receipts increased to $17.6 billion from $16.4 billion, with services exports rising to $38.3 billion. Net transfers — which include remittances from Indian workers overseas — rose to $13.2 billion from $12.6 billion, though net income outflows widened to $6.1 billion from $4 billion.

The RBI's $136 billion machine

The inflow surge traces directly to the RBI's June 5 measures: discounted hedging for overseas borrowings by state-run firms and banks, and free hedging for banks raising overseas foreign-exchange deposits. Reuters reported the schemes mobilised $136.4 billion between June 5 and August 31, with $127 billion coming from non-resident deposits. FCNR-B balances across Indian banks nearly doubled from $32.56 billion on June 5 to $60.55 billion by July 30.

The timing mattered. Worries over the balance of payments have been a key pain point for the rupee in 2026, as the Iran war lifted crude oil prices and triggered unabated capital outflows. The RBI stepped up intervention alongside the inflow push; reserves stood at an all-time high of $729.3 billion in the week ended August 21, and analysts expect them to cross $750 billion by September-end. Some analysts now expect a near-neutral or modest surplus for the fiscal year ending March 2027.

The sceptics' case

Not everyone is convinced the inflows are all fresh. Economists at HDFC Bank and IDFC First Bank have pointed to timing lags in banks swapping deposits with the RBI, hedging of future coupon payments, and possible rebooking of existing FCNR deposits to capture higher yields. RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra has dismissed recirculation concerns as insignificant. Either way, the flows carry rollover risk: today's leveraged deposits must be refinanced or repaid when they mature in three to five years.

What it means for the diaspora

For NRIs, the July data is the clearest evidence yet that the diaspora's savings have become a decisive variable in India's external balance. Gulf-based investors have been the strongest source of demand for the deposit schemes, and the September 30 deadline on the concessional-hedging window makes this a closing — not permanent — opportunity for above-market dollar yields on FCNR-B placements.
